# Metric Topology
## Theorem 1
**(i)** If $d$ is a metric on a set $X$, then the collection $\mathscr{B} = \{ B_d(x, \varepsilon) \mid x \in X, \varepsilon > 0 \}$ is a basis for a topology $\mathscr{T}_d$ on $X$, called ***the metric topology induced by $d$.*** We call $(X, \mathscr{T}_d)$ a ***metric space***.

> A function $d : X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ is said to be a ***metric*** on $X$ if it satisfies the following conditions:
> 
> **(i)** $d(x, y) \geq 0, \forall x, y \in X$, and $d(x, y) = 0$ if and only if $x = y$.
> 
> **(ii)** $d(x, y) = d(y, x), \forall x, y \in X$.
> 
> **(iii)** $d(x, z) \leq d(x, y) + d(y, z), \forall x, y, z \in X$.
>
> The $\varepsilon$-ball centered at $x$ is defined by $B_d(x, \varepsilon) = \{ y \in X \mid d(x, y) < \varepsilon \}$.

해석개론에서는 위상 얘기를 생략하고 바로 거리공간 위에서 오픈이니, 컴팩트이니 등등의 논의를 진행했었다. 위상수학에서는 이를 더 일반화해서 사실 거리공간도 위상공간의 한 종류로 이야기하고, 메트릭으로 만들어지는 오픈볼을 오픈셋으로 볼 수 있게 한다.

$$\begin{align*}
U \in \mathscr{T}_d \iff \forall x \in U, \exists \delta > 0 \text{ such that } B_d(x, \delta) \subset U.
\end{align*}$$

## Definition 1
**(i)** A space $X$ is said to be ***metrizable*** if there exists a metric $d: X \times X \to \mathbb{R}$ that induces the topology of $X$. 

Let $A$ be a subset of a metric space $(X, d)$.

**(ii)** $A$ is said to be ***bounded*** if there is some positive number $M$ such that $d(a, b) \le M, \forall a, b \in A$. 

**(iii)** If $A$ is bounded and nonempty, then the ***diameter*** of $A$ is defined to be the number $\mathrm{diam}(A) = \sup_{a, b \in A} d(a, b)$.

유클리드 공간 $(\mathbb{R}, \mathscr{T}_{\text{usual}})$에 거리 $d(x, y) = \vert x - y \vert$를 부여할 수 있고, 이 거리가 만들어내는 위상은 기존의 유클리드 공간과 정확히 동일하다. 이렇게 기존의 위상 $(X, \mathscr{T})$와 정확히 동일한 위상을 만들어낼 수 있도록 거리 $d$를 잡아올 수 있을 때 $X$를 거리화가능하다고 부르고, 어떤 특정한 거리 $d$가 $X$에 만들어내는 위상공간 $(X, \mathscr{T}_d)$를 거리 공간이라고 부른다. 다시 말해 $(X, \mathscr{T})$가 거리화가능하고, 이에 대응되는 거리 $d$가 존재하면 $(X, \mathscr{T}) = (X, \mathscr{T}_d)$이다. 한편 애초에 처음부터 위상이 존재하고 이 위상을 유도하는 거리가 존재한다는 맥락이 아니라, 처음부터 거리가 주어져서 이 거리가 어떤 위상을 생성할 수도 있고, 이러한 맥락의 정의를 거리공간이라고 부른다.

### Proof
Let $x \in X$. Since $d(x, x) = 0$, we have $x \in B_d(x, \varepsilon), \forall \varepsilon > 0$. Thus, there is $B \in \mathscr{B}$ such that $x \in B$.

Let $x \in B_1 \cap B_2$ for some $B_1, B_2 \in \mathscr{B}$. Then $B_1 = B_d(x_1, \delta_1)$ and $B_2 = B_d(x_2, \delta_2)$ for some $x_1, x_2 \in X$ and $\delta_1, \delta_2 > 0$. Then we see that $x \in B_d(x_1, \delta_1)$ and $x \in B_d(x_2, \delta_2)$, which means that $d(x, x_1) < \delta_1$ and $d(x, x_2) < \delta_2$. Let $\delta = \min \{ \delta_1 - d(x, x_1), \delta_2 - d(x, x_2) \}$. Clearly $\delta > 0$. Then we must have $x \in B_d(x, \delta) \subset B_1 \cap B_2$.

To see this, let $y \in B_d(x, \delta)$. Then $d(x, y) < \delta$, so that $d(x, y) < \delta_1 - d(x, x_1)$ and $d(x, y) < \delta_2 - d(x, x_2)$. Thus, we have 

$$d(y, x_1) \le d(y, x) + d(x, x_1) < \delta_1 \quad \text{and} \quad d(y, x_2) \le d(y, x) + d(x, x_2) < \delta_2,$$

so that $y \in B_d(x_1, \delta_1) \cap B_d(x_2, \delta_2) = B_1 \cap B_2$. Therefore, $B_d(x, \delta) \subset B_1 \cap B_2$. It follows that $\mathscr{B}$ is a basis for a topology on $X$. $\blacksquare$

## Example
The followings give the metrics on $\mathbb{R}^n$:

**(i)** ***The Euclidean metric***: $\displaystyle d(x, y) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - y_i)^2}$.

**(ii)** ***The taxicab metric***: $\displaystyle d(x, y) = \sum_{i=1}^n \vert x_i - y_i \vert$.

**(iii)** ***The square metric***: $\displaystyle d(x, y) = \max _{1 \le i \le n} \{ \vert x_i - y_i \vert \}$.

**(iv)** ***The discrete metric***: 

$$d(x, y) = \begin{cases}
0 & \text{if } x = y \\
1 & \text{if } x \neq y.
\end{cases}$$

## Theorem 2
Let $d, d'$ be two metrics on a set $X$, and let $\mathscr{T}_d, \mathscr{T}_{d'}$ be two topologies induced by $d, d'$, respectively. Then $\mathscr{T}_{d'}$ is finer than $\mathscr{T}_d$ $\iff$ $\forall x \in X$ and $\forall \varepsilon > 0$, $\exists \delta > 0$ such that $B_{d'}(x, \delta) \subset B_d(x, \varepsilon)$.

### Proof
$(\Longrightarrow)$ Suppose that $\mathscr{T}_{d} \subset \mathscr{T}_{d'}$. Let $x \in X$ and $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $B _d(x, \varepsilon)$ is a basis element of $\mathscr{T}_{d}$, [there exists a basis element $B'$ of $\mathscr{T}_{d'}$ such that $x \in B' \subset B _d(x, \varepsilon)$.](../Basis_Topology/index.qmd#sec-theorem-4) Then $B' = B_{d'}(x, \delta)$ for some $\delta > 0$. Thus, we have $B_{d'}(x, \delta) \subset B_d(x, \varepsilon)$.

$(\Longleftarrow)$ Suppose that $\forall x \in X$ and $\forall \varepsilon > 0$, $\exists \delta > 0$ such that $B_{d'}(x, \delta) \subset B _d(x, \varepsilon)$. Let $B$ be a basis element of $\mathscr{T}_{d}$. Then $B = B_{d}(x, \varepsilon)$ for some $x \in X$ and $\varepsilon > 0$. By assumption, $\exists \delta > 0$ such that $B_{d'}(x, \delta) \subset B_d(x, \varepsilon)$. Since $B_{d'}(x, \delta)$ is a basis element of $\mathscr{T}_{d'}$ and it contains $x$, we conclude that $\mathscr{T}_{d} \subset \mathscr{T}_{d'}$. $\blacksquare$

## Corollary
**(i)** Let $d, d', d''$ be the Euclidean metric, the taxicab metric, and the square metric, respectively, on $\mathbb{R}^n$. Then $\mathscr{T}_d = \mathscr{T}_{d'} = \mathscr{T}_{d''}$. Furthermore, these topologies are the same as the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

**(ii)** Let $d$ be a discrete metric on a set $X$. Then the metric topology induced by $d$ is the discrete topology on $X$.

::: {.callout-note title="Proof" collapse="true" icon=false}
**(i)** Let $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $\varepsilon > 0$.

**1.** $\mathscr{T} _d \subset \mathscr{T} _{d'}$

We claim that $B _{d'}(x, \varepsilon) \subset B _{d}(x, \varepsilon)$.

To verify this, let $y \in B _{d'}(x, \varepsilon)$. Then we have

$$d(x, y) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - y_i)^2} \le \sum_{i=1}^n \vert x_i - y_i \vert = d'(x, y) < \varepsilon,$$ 

so that $y \in B_d(x, \varepsilon)$. Thus, we have $B _{d'}(x, \varepsilon) \subset B _{d}(x, \varepsilon)$, and therefore $\mathscr{T} _d \subset \mathscr{T} _{d'}$ by Theoerm 2.

**2.** $\mathscr{T} _{d'} \subset \mathscr{T} _{d''}$

Take $\delta = \frac{\varepsilon}{n}$. We claim that $B _{d''}(x, \delta) \subset B _{d'}(x, \varepsilon)$.

To verify this, let $y \in B _{d''}(x, \delta)$. Then we have

$$\vert x_i - y_i \vert \le \max_{1 \le i \le n} \vert x_i - y_i \vert < \delta,$$

for all $i = 1, 2, \cdots, n$, which implies that 

$$d'(x, y) = \sum_{i=1}^n \vert x_i - y_i \vert < n \max_{1 \le i \le n} \vert x_i - y_i \vert < n \delta = n \frac{\varepsilon}{n} = \varepsilon.$$

Hence, $y \in B_{d'}(x, \varepsilon)$, so that $B_{d''}(x, \delta) \subset B_{d'}(x, \varepsilon)$. Therefore, $\mathscr{T} _{d'} \subset \mathscr{T} _{d''}$ by Theoerm 2.

**3.** $\mathscr{T} _{d''} \subset \mathscr{T} _{d}$

Take $\delta = \varepsilon$. We claim that $B _{d}(x, \delta) \subset B _{d''}(x, \varepsilon)$.

To verify this, let $y \in B _{d}(x, \delta)$. Then we have

$$d''(x, y) = \max_{1 \le i \le n} \vert x_i - y_i \vert < \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - y_i)^2} < \delta = \varepsilon$$

Hence, $y \in B_{d''}(x, \varepsilon)$, so that $B_{d}(x, \delta) \subset B_{d''}(x, \varepsilon)$. Therefore, $\mathscr{T} _{d''} \subset \mathscr{T} _{d}$ by Theoerm 2. 

Thus, we have $\mathscr{T} _d = \mathscr{T} _{d'} = \mathscr{T} _{d''}$. 

To show that these topologies are the same as the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}^n$, it suffices to show for the case $\mathscr{T}_d$. 

Let 

$$B := \prod_{i=1}^n (a_i, b_i)$$

be a basis element of the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}^n$, and let $x \in B$. For each $i = 1, 2, ..., n$, there exists $\varepsilon_i > 0$ such that $x_i \in (x_i - \varepsilon_i, x_i + \varepsilon_i) \subset (a_i, b_i)$. Let $\varepsilon := \min _{1 \le i \le n} \varepsilon_i$. Then we claim that $x \in B_d(x, \varepsilon) \subset B$. 

To see this, let $y \in B_d(x, \varepsilon)$. Then $d(x, y) < \varepsilon$, which means that 

$$\vert x_i - y_i \vert \le \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-y_i)^2} < \varepsilon \le \varepsilon_i$$

for each $i = 1, 2, ..., n$. Then $y_i \in (x_i - \varepsilon_i, x_i + \varepsilon_i) \subset (a_i, b_i)$ for each $i = 1,2, ..., n$, which implies that $y \in B$. Thus, $x \in B_d(x, \varepsilon) \subset B$, and therefore $\mathscr{T}_d$ is finer than the usual topology.

Conversely, let $B_d(x, \varepsilon)$ be a basis element of $\mathscr{T}_d$, and let $y \in B_d(x, \varepsilon)$. Then $y \in B_d(y, \delta) \subset B_d(x, \varepsilon)$ for some $\delta > 0$. Take 

$$B := \prod_{i=1}^n \left(y_i - \frac{\delta}{\sqrt{n}}, y_i + \frac{\delta}{\sqrt{n}} \right).$$

Then $B$ is open in the usual topology, and $y \in B$. We claim that $y \in B \subset B_d(y, \delta) \subset B_d(x, \varepsilon)$, so that the usual topology is finer than $\mathscr{T}_d$.

To see this, let $z \in B$. Then we have that $z_i \in \left(y_i - \frac{\delta}{\sqrt{n}}, y_i + \frac{\delta}{\sqrt{n}} \right)$, which means that $\vert z_i - y_i \vert < \frac{\delta}{\sqrt{n}}$, for each $i = 1, 2, ..., n$. Then we obtain

$$\begin{align*}
d(z, y) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^n (z_i - y_i)^2} < \sqrt{n\left( \frac{\delta}{\sqrt{n}} \right)^2} = \delta,
\end{align*}$$

so that $z \in B_d(y, \delta)$. Thus, $B \subset B_d(y, \delta)$, and therefore $\mathscr{T}_d$ and the usual topology of $\mathbb{R}^n$ are the same. Hence, all of $\mathscr{T}_d, \mathscr{T}_{d'}, \mathscr{T}_{d''}$ and the usual topology are the same. 

**(ii)** Let $U$ be an open set of the discrete topology on $X$, and let $x \in U$. Note that 

$$B_d(x, \varepsilon) = \begin{cases}
\{ x \} & \text{if } \varepsilon \le 1 \\
X & \text{of } \varepsilon > 1
\end{cases}$$

by the definition of the discrete metric. [Thus, we always have $x \in B_d(x, 1) = \\{ x \\} \subset U$, and therefore, the discrete topology on $X$ is the metric topology induced by $d$.](../Basis_Topology/index.qmd#sec-theorem-3) $\blacksquare$
:::

## Theorem 3
**(i)** Every metric space is Hausdorff.

**(ii)** Let $\mathbb{R}^n$ be the metric space with the Euclidean metric $d$. A subspace $A$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$ is [compact](../Compact_Space/index.qmd#sec-definition) $\iff$ $A$ is [closed](../Closed_Set/index.qmd#sec-definition) and bounded.

### Proof
**(i)** Let $X$ be a metric space with the metric $d$. Let $x, y \in X$ with $x \neq y$. Then $d(x, y) > 0$. Take $\varepsilon = \frac{1}{2}d(x, y)$. Since

$$B_d(x, \varepsilon) \cap B_d(y, \varepsilon) = \emptyset$$

and each $B_d(x, \varepsilon), B_d(y, \varepsilon)$ is open in $X$, $X$ is Hausdorff. 

**(ii)**$(\implies)$ Suppose that $A$ is compact. [Since $(\mathbb{R}^n, d)$ is Hausdorff by **(i)**, $A$ is closed.](../Compact_Space/index.qmd#sec-theorem) Consider the open cover $\{ B_d(\mathbf{0}, n) \mid n \in \mathbb{N} \}$ of $A$. Since $A$ is compact, there is a finite subcover $\{ B_d(\mathbf{0}, n_1), \dots, B_d(\mathbf{0}, n_k) \}$ of $A$ for some $n_1, \dots, n_k \in \mathbb{N}$. Let $M = max \{ n_1, \dots, n_k \}$. Then 

$$A \subset \bigcup_{i=1}^k B_d(\mathbf{0}, n_i) \subset B_d(\mathbf{0}, M),$$

which implies that 

$$d(a, b) \le d(a, \mathbf{0}) + d(b, \mathbf{0}) < 2M, \forall a, b \in A.$$

Thus, $A$ is bounded.

$(\impliedby)$ Suppose that $A$ is closed and bounded. Then $d(a, b) < M, \forall a, b \in A$ for some $M > 0$. Choose $x \in A$, and set $N = d(\mathbf{0}, x)$. Since $d(\mathbf{0}, a) \le d(\mathbf{0}, x) + d(x, a) < N+M, \forall a \in A$, we obtain 

$$A \subset B_d(\mathbf{0}, N+M) \subset [-(N+M), N+M]^n.$$

[Since $[-(N+M), N+M]^n$ is compact and $A$ is closed, $A$ is compact.](../Compact_Space/index.qmd#sec-theorem) $\blacksquare$

## Theorem 4
**(i)** Let $f: (X, d_X) \to (Y, d_Y)$ be a function. Then 

$$f \text{ is continuous } \iff \forall x \in X, \forall \varepsilon > 0, \exists \delta >0 \text{ such that } d_X(x, y) < \delta \implies d_Y(f(x), f(y)) < \varepsilon.$$

**(ii)** Let $A$ be a subset of a space $X$. If there exists a sequence of points of $A$ converging to $x \in X$, then $x \in \overline{A}$. Moreover, if $X$ is metrizable, then the converse holds.

**(iii)** Let $f: X \to Y$ be a continuous function. Then for every sequence $\{ x_n \} _{n=1} ^{\infty}$ in $X$ with $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = x$, we have $\lim_{n \to \infty} f(x_n) = f(x)$. Moreover, if $X$ is metrizable, then the converse holds. 

**(iv)** Let $f: (X, d_X) \to (Y, d_Y)$ be a continuous function such that $X$ is compact. Then $f$ is uniformly continuous, i.e. for any $\varepsilon >0$, there exists $\delta > 0$ such that $d_X(x, y) < \delta \implies d_Y(f(x), f(y)) < \varepsilon$. 

### Proof
**(i)**

$(\Longrightarrow)$ Suppose that $f$ is continuous. Let $x \in X$ and $\varepsilon > 0$. Note that $B _{d_Y}(f(x), \varepsilon)$ is open in $Y$ and $f(x) \in B _{d_Y}(f(x), \varepsilon)$. Since $f$ is continuous, there exists a neighborhood $U$ of $x$ such that $f(U) \subset B _{d_Y}(f(x), \varepsilon)$. Since $x \in U$, $x \in B _{d_X}(x, \delta) \subset U$ for some $\delta > 0$. If $y \in B _{d_X}(x, \delta) \subset U$, which implies that $d_X(x, y) < \delta$, then we have $f(y) \in f(U) \subset B _{d_Y}(f(x), \varepsilon)$, so that $d_Y(f(x), f(y)) < \varepsilon$. 

$(\Longleftarrow)$ Suppose that the statement holds. Let $x \in X$ and let $V$ be a neighborhood of $f(x)$. Since $f(x) \in V$, $f(x) \in B _{d_Y}(f(x), \varepsilon) \subset V$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$. By assumtion, $\exists \delta > 0$ such that $d_X(x, y) < \delta \implies d_Y(f(x), f(y)) < \varepsilon.$ Take $U := B _{d_X}(x, \delta)$. Then $U$ is a neighborhood of $x$, and we have 

$$f(U) \subset B _{d_Y}(f(x), \varepsilon) \subset V.$$

Thus, $f$ is continuous.

**(ii)**

$(\Longrightarrow)$ Suppose that there exists a sequence $\{ x_n \}_{n=1}^\infty$ of points of $A$ converging to $x \in X$. Let $U$ be a neighborhood of $x$. Then there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n \in U, \forall n \ge N$. Then $A \cap U \neq \emptyset$, which means that $x \in \overline{A}$.

$(\Longleftarrow)$ Let $X$ be a metric space with a metric $d$. Let $x \in \overline{A}$.  Then $A \cap U \neq \emptyset$ for each neighborhood $U$ of $x$. For each $n \in \mathbb{N}$, we choose an element $x_n$ in $A \cap B_d\left( x, \frac{1}{n} \right)$.

Let $U$ be a neighborhood of $x$. Since $x \in U$, then $x \in B_d(x, \varepsilon) \subset U$ for some $\varepsilon > 0$. Note that $\frac{1}{N} < \varepsilon$ for some $N \in \mathbb{N}$. Then we have $x_n \in B_d\left(x, \frac{1}{n} \right) \subset B_d(x, \varepsilon) \subset U, \forall n \ge N$, and $x_n \in A, \forall n \in \mathbb{N}$. Thus, $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = x$. 

**(iii)** 

$(\Longrightarrow)$ Let $\{ x_n \}_{n=1}^\infty$ be a sequence such that $x_n \in X, \forall n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = x$. Let $V$ be a neighborhood of $f(x)$. Note that $x \in f^{-1}(V)$ and $f^{-1}(V)$ is open in $X$ because $f$ is continuous. Then $\exists N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $x_n \in f^{-1}(V), \forall n \ge N$, which implies that $f(x_n) \in V, \forall n \ge N$. Thus, $\lim_{n \to \infty} f(x_n) = f(x)$.

$(\Longleftarrow)$ Let $X$ be a metric space with a metric $d$. Suppose that the statement holds. Let $A \subset X$, and let $y \in f(\overline{A})$. Then $y = f(x)$ for some $x \in \overline{A}$. Then there exists a sequence $\{ x_n \}_{n=1}^\infty$ such that $x_n \in A, \forall n \in \mathbb{N}$ and $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = x \in X$ by the preceeding theorem. By assumption, we have $\lim_{n \to \infty} f(x_n) = f(x)$ and $f(x_n) \in f(A), \forall n \in \mathbb{N}$. By the preceeding theorem, we have $y = f(x) \in \overline{f(A)}$, which means that $f(\overline{A}) \subset \overline{f(A)}$. Hence, $f$ is continuous. 

**(iv)** Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Then $\left\{ B_d \left(y, \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \right) \,\, \Big \vert \,\, y \in Y \right\}$ is an [open cover](../Compact_Space/index.qmd#sec-definition) of $Y$. Since $f$ is continuous, the collection $\mathcal{U} = \left\{ f^{-1} \left( B_d \left(y, \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \right) \right) \,\, \Big \vert \,\, y \in Y \right\}$ is an open cover of $X$. Since $X$ is compact, it has a [Lebesgue number](../Lebesgue_Number/index.qmd#sec-definition) $\delta$ for $\mathcal{U}$.

Let $x, y \in X$. If $d(x, y) < \delta$, then the subset $\{ x, y \}$ has the [diameter](../Lebesgue_Number/index.qmd#sec-definition) less than $\delta$, which implies that $\{ x, y \} \subset f^{-1} \left( B_d \left(z, \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \right) \right)$ for some $z \in Y$. Thus, $f(x), f(y) \in B_d \left(z, \frac{\varepsilon}{2} \right)$, so that

$$d_Y(f(x), f(y)) \le d_Y(f(x), z) + d_Y(f(y), z) < \frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon.$$

Hence, $f$ is uniformly continuous. $\blacksquare$

# Complete Space
Let $(X, d)$ be a metric space.

**(i)** A sequence $\{ x_n \}$ in $X$ is called a ***Cauchy sequence*** in $(X, d)$ if $\forall \varepsilon > 0, \exists N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $d(x_n, x_m) < \varepsilon, \forall n, m \ge N$.

**(ii)** $(X, d)$ is said to be ***complete*** if every Cauchy sequence in $X$ converges.

## Remark
**(i)** Every convergent sequence in $X$ is a Cauchy sequence. However, the converse does not hold in general.

::: {.callout-note title="Example" collapse="true" icon=false}
1. The sequence $x_n = \left( 1 + \frac{1}{n} \right)^n$ is a Cauchy sequence in $(\mathbb{Q}, d_{\text{Euclidean}})$ but it does not converge in $(\mathbb{Q}, d_{\text{Euclidean}})$.

2. The sequence $x_n = \frac{1}{n}$ is a Cauchy sequence in $((0, 2), d_{\text{Euclidean}})$ but it does not converge in $((0, 2), d_{\text{Euclidean}})$.
:::

**(ii)** If $(X, d)$ is complete, then a sequence $\{ x_n \}$ is Cauchy $\iff$ $\{ x_n \}$ is convergent.

**(iii)** $(\mathbb{R}^n, d)$ is not complete in general.

::: {.callout-note title="Example" collapse="true" icon=false}

:::

## Theorem 5
Let $(X, d)$ be a metric space.

**(i)** Every closed subset of a complete metric space if complete.

**(ii)** $(X, d)$ is complete $\iff$ $(X, \overline{d})$ is complete, where $\overline{d}(x, y) = \min \{ d(x, y), 1 \}$.

**(iii)** $(X, d)$ is complete if every Cauchy sequence in $X$ has a convergent subsequence.

**(iv)** $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_{\text{Euclidean}})$ is complete.

**(v)** There is a metric $D$ for $\mathbb{R}^\omega$ such that $(\mathbb{R}^\omega, D)$ is complete.

### Proof
**(i)** Let $C$ be a closed subset of a complete metric space $X$, and let $\{ x_n \}$ be a Cauchy sequence in $C$. Since $X$ is complete, $\{ x_n \}$ converges to $x \in X$. By Theorem 4 **(ii)**, $x \in \overline{C} = C$. Thus, $C$ is complete.

**(ii)**

**(iii)** Suppose that a Cauchy sequence $\{ x_n \}$ in $X$ has a convergent subsequence $\{ x_{n_k} \}$ with $x_{n_k} \to x$. Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Then there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $d(x_n, x_m) < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ and $d(x_n, x) < \frac{\varepsilon}{2}$ for all $n, m \ge N$. Then we have 

$$d(x_n, x) \le d(x_n, x_{n_k}) + d(x_{n_k}, x) < \frac{\varepsilon}{2} + \frac{\varepsilon}{2} = \varepsilon, \forall n \ge N.$$

Thus, $\lim_{n \to \infty} x_n = x$, and therefore $(X, d)$ is complete.

**(iv)** Let $\{ x_n \}$ be a Cauchy sequence of $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_{\text{Euclidean}})$. Then there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\vert x_n, x_m \vert < 1, \forall n, m \ge N$. Let $M := \max \{ \vert x_1 \vert, \dots, \vert x_N \vert \}$, and let $C := \{ x \in \mathbb{R}^n \mid \vert x vert \le M + 1 \}$. Since $1 > \vert x_n, x_N \vert \ge \vert x_n \vert - \vert x_N \vert, \forall n \ge N$, we have $\vert x_n \vert < \vert x_N \vert + 1, \forall n \ge N$. Thus, $x_n \in C, \forall n \in \mathbb{N}$. Since $C$ is closed and bounded, $C$ is compact, which means that $\{ x_n \}$ has a convergent subsequence. By **(iii)**, $(\mathbb{R}^n, d_{\text{Euclidean}})$ is complete.

**(v)** Let $\bar{d}(a, b) := \min \{ d(a, b), 1 \}$ be the standard bounded metric on $\mathbb{R}$, where $d(a, b) = \vert a - b \vert$. Since $(\mathbb{R}, d)$ is complete, so is $(\mathbb{R}, \bar{d})$ by **(ii)**.

Let $D$ be the metric on $\mathbb{R}^\omega$ defined by 

$$D(\mathbf{x}, \mathbf{y}) = \sup_{n \in \mathbb{N}} \left \{ \frac{\bar{d}(x_n, y_n)}{n} \right \}.$$

Since $\frac{\bar{d}(x_n, y_n)}{n} \le \frac{1}{n} \le 1, \forall n \in \mathbb{N}$, $D$ is well-defined. Note that the metric $D$ induces the product space $\mathbb{R}^\omega$.

Let $\{ \mathbf{x}_n \}$ be a Cauchy sequence in $(\mathbb{R}^\omega, D)$. Consider the sequence $\{ \pi_{n_0}(\mathbf{x}_n) \}_{n=1}^\infty$ in $(\mathbb{R}, \bar{d})$ for some fixed $n_0 \in \mathbb{N}$. Let $\varepsilon > 0$. Since $\{ \mathbf{x}_n \}$ is a Cauchy sequence, there exists $N \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $D(\mathbf{x}_n, \mathbf{x}_m) < \frac{\varepsilon}{n_0}, \forall n, m \ge N$. Then for all $n, m \ge N$, we have

$$\bar{d}(\pi_{n_0}(\mathbf{x}_n), \pi_{n_0}(\mathbf{x}_m)) \le D(\mathbf{x}_n, \mathbf{x}_m) \cdot n_0 < \frac{\varepsilon}{n_0} \cdot n_0 = \varepsilon,$$

which means that the sequence $\{ \pi_{n_0}(\mathbf{x}_n) \}_{n=1}^\infty$ is a Cauchy sequence in $(\mathbb{R}, \bar{d})$.

Since $(\mathbb{R}, \bar{d})$ is complete, $\{ \pi_{n_0}(\mathbf{x}_n) \}_{n=1}^\infty$ converges.

Suppose that $\{ \pi_{i}(\mathbf{x}_n) \}_{n=1}^\infty$ converges to $a_i \in \mathbb{R}$ for each $i \in \mathbb{N}$, and let $\mathbf{a} = (a_1, a_2, a_3, \dots) \in \mathbb{R}^\omega$.

Let $U = \prod_{i \in \mathbb{N}} U_i$ be a basis element of $(\mathbb{R}^\omega, D)$ containing $\mathbf{a}$, where each $U_i$ is an open subset of $\mathbb{R}$ containing $\pi_i(\mathbf{a})$. Then there exist finitely many indices $i_1, \dots, i_k$ such that $U_{i_j} \subsetneq \mathbb{R}$. For each $j = 1, \dots, k$, there exists $N_{i_j} \in \mathbb{N}$ such that $\pi_{i_j}(\mathbf{x}_n) \in U_{i_j}, \forall n \ge N_{i_j}$. Let $N = \max \{ N_{i_1}, \dots, N_{i_k} \}$. Then 

$$\mathbf{x}_n \in U, \forall n \ge N,$$

which means that $\mathbf{x}_n \to \mathbf{a}$. Hence, $(\mathbb{R}^\omega, D)$ is complete. $\blacksquare$

# Reference
- James R. Munkres. (2000). Topology (2nd ed.). Pearson.
